title: Saving Babies? Revisiting the Effect of Very Low Birth Weight Classification on Mortality
research_question: Do expansions of public health insurance eligibility to low-income nondisabled adults reduce mortality and improve access to care and self-reported health? Specifically, what is the causal effect on all-cause mortality, insurance coverage, cost-related delays in care, and self-rated health among working-age adults?
data_description: The study uses three data sources covering 1997–2007. County-level all-cause mortality for adults aged 20–64 (stratified by age, race, and sex) comes from the CDC Compressed Mortality File, yielding 68,012 county-year-demographic observations. Individual-level data on Medicaid coverage, uninsurance, and self-reported health status come from the Current Population Survey (169,124 persons aged 19–64), and data on cost-related delays in needed care come from the Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (192,148 persons). County-year economic covariates (poverty rate, unemployment rate, median household income) come from the Area Resource File. The sample spans five years before and five years after each state's policy change, with units of observation being county-year demographic cells for mortality and individuals for survey outcomes.
institutional_context: Traditional Medicaid in the United States covered low-income children, parents, pregnant women, and disabled persons but generally excluded nondisabled childless adults. Between 2000 and 2005, three states substantially broadened eligibility to cover this group: Arizona (November 2001, childless adults up to 100% of the federal poverty level, plus parents up to 200% FPL in October 2002), Maine (October 2002, childless adults up to 100% FPL), and New York (September 2001, childless adults up to 100% FPL and parents up to 150% FPL). Neighboring states without such expansions—New Hampshire, Pennsylvania, Nevada, and New Mexico—were chosen as comparisons based on geographic proximity and demographic similarity. This setting precedes and informs the Affordable Care Act's 2014 nationwide eligibility expansion to adults up to 138% FPL, which states could opt into following the Supreme Court ruling.
